analysis.one_liner: Bans abusive terms like balloon payments and prepayment penalties on high-cost home loans and requires plain-language risk disclosures.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it was referred to the House Banking Committee's consumer credit subcommittee in January 1995 and died there with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to define a category of "high cost mortgages" — loans with rates far above market, huge fees at closing, or payments eating most of the borrower's income — and impose rules on them: lenders must give borrowers clear written warnings three days before closing that they could lose their home, and loans could no longer include prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization, or stacked refinancing fees. It would also let borrowers recover all finance charges and fees if a lender breaks the rules, let state attorneys general sue violators, and hold investors who buy these loans on the hook for the lender's misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners, especially older and lower-income borrowers targeted with high-fee refinancing loans secured by their homes, would get plain warnings before closing and protection from the loan features that most often strip home equity. If a lender violated the rules, the borrower could recover all the finance charges and fees paid, and state attorneys general could sue on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a conspicuous written warning, given at least three business days before closing, that the borrower could lose the home and all money put into it if they fail to meet loan obligations [S3].

Prohibits high-cost mortgages from containing prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization, and prepaid consolidated payments, and blocks the same lender or its affiliate from charging points or fees again when refinancing the same loan [S3].
If a lender fails to comply, the borrower can recover all finance charges and fees paid on the loan, and the assignee who bought the loan is subject to the borrower's claims and defenses [S3].
State attorneys general are empowered to bring enforcement actions in court within five years of a violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and mortgage brokers originating high-cost loans would lose some of their most profitable fee streams — points and closing fees above 8% of the loan, prepayment penalties, and repeat refinancing charges — and would face disclosure requirements, civil liability, and possible lawsuits from state attorneys general.

drawbacks.text: Banning prepayment penalties and limiting fees on the riskiest loans could make some lenders stop serving borrowers with damaged credit, reducing access to credit for the very households the bill targets — the standard trade-off of predatory-lending rules.

The compliance and litigation exposure — with assignee liability reaching investors who buy the loans — could raise the cost of legitimate subprime lending, which honest supporters would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target a narrow slice of lending — loans more than 10 points above Treasury rates, fees over 8% of the loan, or debt payments above 60% of income — so the benefit to ordinary homeowners in that segment is large and the cost falls on lenders whose profits depend on those features. The main honest objection is that some risky borrowers might lose access to credit, but the bill's own structure (limited exceptions, a 90-day prepayment allowance) shows an attempt to balance that.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced the first day of the new Congress, it was sent to the House Banking Committee and then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, no markup, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edolphus Towns introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day [S5].
On January 27, 1995, it was referred to the subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders and brokers are better off: none of the proposed limits on prepayment penalties, balloon payments, closing fees, or assignee liability took effect, so their existing loan practices continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 4, 1995 and never reported it out; it was passed to a subcommittee and no hearing or markup was held.

against.name: Rep. James Leach
against.role: Chair, House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: As the newly installed committee chair in the Republican-controlled 104th Congress, controlled the committee calendar on which the bill died without a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, in a Congress newly controlled by Republicans, so no bipartisan or partisan bloc ever formed around it [S4].

industries.industry: High-cost and subprime mortgage lenders and brokers
industries.note: These lenders profit from the exact features the bill bans — points and fees above 8% of the loan, prepayment penalties, balloon payments, and repeat refinancing charges on home equity loans. The bill's failure left that fee structure intact.

industries.industry: Investors and assignees who buy high-cost mortgages
industries.note: The bill would have made loan buyers liable for the borrower's claims against the original lender, raising the cost of packaging these loans. Because it died, the secondary market for high-cost loans faced no such liability.
